title: Complementary quotient for idempotent localizations away from an ideal
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $K=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\subseteq R$ be an ideal generated by finitely many elements (allowing $r=0$), and let $u:R\to E$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings. For $f\in R$ write $R_f$ and $E_f$ for localization at the powers of $f$ and $u(f)$ respectively [def-weil-ring-localization-away]. Suppose that for every $f\in K$ there is an idempotent $e_f\in R_f$, meaning $e_f^2=e_f$, such that $u_f:R_f\to E_f$ identifies $E_f$ with $(R_f)_{e_f}$ as an $R_f$-algebra. Then there is a surjective ring homomorphism $v:R\twoheadrightarrow E^{\prime}$ such that, for every $f\in K$, the homomorphism $(u,v)_f:R_f\to(E\times E^{\prime})_f$ is an isomorphism.

proof.text: If $r=0$, then $K=0$. Take $E^{\prime}=R$ and $v=\mathrm{id}_R$. The only $f\in K$ is $0$, and localization at $0$ is the zero ring: the fraction equality of [def-weil-ring-localization-away] identifies every fraction with $0$. Thus both sides of $(u,v)_0$ are zero rings and it is an isomorphism. In the remaining steps assume $r>0$ and choose the given idempotents $e_i=e_{f_i}$.

source.place: Tag 0C2A, lemma-glueing-sum-components-open; the empty generating list made explicit

proof.text: Write $e_i=c_i/f_i^{d_i}$. Since $e_i^2=e_i$, the fraction equality of [def-weil-ring-localization-away] gives an integer $k_i\geq0$ with $f_i^{k_i}(c_i^2-f_i^{d_i}c_i)=0$. Choose $t_i\geq k_i$ and put $a_i=f_i^{t_i}c_i$, $n_i=d_i+t_i$. Then $a_i^2-f_i^{n_i}a_i=f_i^{2t_i}(c_i^2-f_i^{d_i}c_i)=0$, while $e_i=a_i/f_i^{n_i}$. Choose one $n\geq\max_i n_i$ and replace $a_i$ by $f_i^{n-n_i}a_i$. This preserves the represented fractions and gives $a_i^2=f_i^na_i$ and $e_i=a_i/f_i^n$ for every $i$. These are equalities in $R$, not merely in $R_{f_i}$.

source.place: Tag 0C2A, proof: choose a common n and clear the idempotence relations

proof.text: For each pair $i,j$ put $B=R_{f_if_j}$ and denote the images of $e_i,e_j$ in $B$ by the same letters. Inverting $f_j$ in the given $R_{f_i}$-algebra identification, and conversely inverting $f_i$ for $j$, identifies the same structural map $B\to E_{f_if_j}$ with both $B\to B_{e_i}$ and $B\to B_{e_j}$. The order of these localizations does not matter: their maps send an iterated fraction to the fraction with the multiplied denominators, and the inverse maps are determined by making both denominators units [def-weil-ring-localization-away]. An invertible idempotent equals $1$, so $e_i-1$ maps to $0$ in $B_{e_j}$. The zero-fraction criterion gives $e_j^k(e_i-1)=0$ for some $k$, which we may increase to at least $1$. As $e_j^k=e_j$, this says $e_ie_j=e_j$. Interchanging $i,j$ gives $e_ie_j=e_i$. Therefore $e_i=e_j$ in $R_{f_if_j}$.

source.place: Tag 0C2A, proof: compatibility of the idempotent localizations on pairwise overlaps, with both orders written out

proof.text: In $R_{f_if_j}$ the fractions representing $e_i,e_j$ have common denominator $(f_if_j)^n$ and numerators $f_j^na_i,f_i^na_j$. By [def-weil-ring-localization-away], for each pair some power of $f_if_j$ kills $f_j^na_i-f_i^na_j$. Since there are finitely many pairs, choose a single $N\geq0$ with $(f_if_j)^N(f_j^na_i-f_i^na_j)=0$ for all $i,j$. Put $b_i=f_i^Na_i$ and $d=n+N$. Rearranging this equality yields $f_j^db_i=f_i^db_j$ in $R$. Also $b_i^2=f_i^{2N}a_i^2=f_i^{2N+n}a_i=f_i^db_i$ and $e_i=b_i/f_i^d$. Hence in $R_{f_i}$, each $b_j$ is the multiple $(f_j^d/f_i^d)b_i$ of $b_i$.

source.place: Tag 0C2A, proof: uniform rescaling to put every numerator in the ideal of each localized numerator; symmetric overlap equality simplifies the exponents

proof.text: Set $J=(b_1,\ldots,b_r)\subseteq R$, $E^{\prime}=R/J$, and let $v:R\twoheadrightarrow R/J$ be the quotient map. The preceding divisibility gives $JR_{f_i}=(b_i)=(e_i)$ for every $i$, since $f_i$ is invertible in $R_{f_i}$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-localization-quotient-commute] with $B=R$, the ideal $J$, and $b=f_i$. It identifies $E^{\prime}_{f_i}$, compatibly with $v_{f_i}$, with $R_{f_i}/JR_{f_i}=R_{f_i}/(e_i)$.

source.place: Tag 0C2A, proof: construction of C prime and its localizations; Tag 00CT, proposition-localize-quotient

proof.text: For $B=R_{f_i}$ and its idempotent $e=e_i$, the canonical map $B\to B_e\times B/(e)$ is an isomorphism. Indeed [def-weil-ring-localization-away] identifies $B_e$ with the ring $eB$ (whose identity is $e$) by $x/e^m\mapsto ex$; its inverse sends $ex$ to $ex/1$. Likewise $B/(e)\to(1-e)B$, $[y]\mapsto(1-e)y$, has inverse $(1-e)y\mapsto[(1-e)y]$. The maps are well defined by the fraction equality and $e(1-e)=0$. Under these identifications the canonical map is $b\mapsto(eb,(1-e)b)$, with inverse $(x,y)\mapsto x+y$, since $e+(1-e)=1$ and $e(1-e)=0$. The hypothesis $E_{f_i}=B_e$ and step 5 therefore show that the canonical map $R_{f_i}\to E_{f_i}\times E^{\prime}_{f_i}$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Tag 0C2A, proof: the elementary product decomposition B = B_e times B/(e), with inverse specified

proof.text: Write $T=E\times E^{\prime}$ and $\alpha=(u,v):R\to T$. Localization at any $h\in R$ commutes with this two-factor product: the map $T_h\to E_h\times E^{\prime}_h$ sends $(x,y)/h^k$ to $(x/h^k,y/h^k)$, and its inverse sends $(x/h^k,y/h^l)$ to $(h^lx,h^ky)/h^{k+l}$, with the powers of $h$ acting through the respective structural maps. The fraction equality of [def-weil-ring-localization-away] checks independence of representatives and both composites. Thus step 6 gives exactly the required isomorphism $\alpha_{f_i}:R_{f_i}\to T_{f_i}$, not a different map with the same source and target. Further localization preserves these isomorphisms by applying the inverse maps to numerators and denominators.

source.place: Tag 0C2A, proof: interpretation of the product-localization map and further localization

proof.text: Fix any $f\in K$, put $S=R_f$, $V=T_f$, and let $g_i=f_i/1\in S$. Writing $f=\sum_i c_if_i$ shows $1=\sum_i(c_i/f)g_i$, so the $g_i$ generate the unit ideal in $S$. Iterated fractions identify $S_{g_i}$ with $R_{ff_i}$ and $V_{g_i}$ with $T_{ff_i}$. Thus step 7 gives an isomorphism $\alpha_i:S_{g_i}\to V_{g_i}$ for each $i$, and also on every overlap. Regard $S,V$ as $S$-modules; their module localizations are these ring localizations by the same fraction formulas [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away, def-weil-ring-localization-away]. If $s\in\ker\alpha_f$, then all $s/1=0$ because the $\alpha_i$ are injective. The injectivity clause of [lem-weil-pbc-cover-module-exact] for $M=S$ gives $s=0$. For $t\in V$, take $s_i=\alpha_i^{-1}(t/1)$. On overlaps their images coincide, because their images under the overlap isomorphism are both the restriction of $t$. The gluing clause of that node for $M=S$ gives $s\in S$ with $s/1=s_i$. Now $\alpha_f(s)-t$ is zero in every $V_{g_i}$; the injectivity clause for $M=V$ gives $\alpha_f(s)=t$. Hence $\alpha_f$ is bijective and so a ring isomorphism, for every $f\in K$.
